Secure cloud storage is the cheaper, safer alternative to keeping files physical

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (525 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, physical storage and memory are only getting more expensive, but that doesn’t mean we need to store any less.
  • Based in Switzerland and operating out of data centers in the EU and US, pCloud is relied on by over 24 million owners across the globe.
  • According to recent reports, that extends throughout every platform it’s available on, including Android, iOS, macOS, Windows, and Linux.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, physical storage and memory are only getting more expensive, but that doesn’t mean we need to store any less. The alternative solution is a secure cloud storage platform, and there’s really only one good option.

Based in Switzerland and operating out of data centers in the EU and US, pCloud is relied on by over 24 million owners across the globe. Its standard for security comes naturally high, given where it’s based. Swiss law sets the standard for data privacy and consumer rights, and pCloud’s entire foundation sits on security and privacy, with a 13-year history to back it up.

According to recent reports, that extends throughout every platform it’s available on, including Android, iOS, macOS, Windows, and Linux. On just about any platform, people get access to the pCloud Drive app for dedicated storage and backup. On Android and iOS, you have an additional option to automatically back up photos to free up space on your phone. pCloud Photos also acts as a smart photo gallery within the app, and sharing between other pCloud users and friends is made incredibly simple.

Sources indicate that no matter where you access your pCloud Drive, all your files are there – safe and secure. You can store all kinds of files in pCloud, including documents, photos, videos, and even documents containing passwords.

Of course, you also get the option to take security a step further with pCloud Encryption. Your most sensitive files can be stored with an added layer of client-side, zero-knowledge encryption. The key is all yours, and no one else’s.

Even if you already have a hefty backup solution like an in-home NAS, pCloud is still a good option because it makes that NAS that much more useful. It has an official NAS backup feature with support for WebDAV, Rsync, SFTP, and SCP. pCloud simply provides another safety net for your existing backup.

Industry observers note that unlike a lot of cloud storage services, pCloud doesn’t charge on a monthly or even yearly basis. Just like buying physical storage, paying once for what you need is enough. But what makes it a better option than going the traditional route – beyond the skyrocketing storage prices – is the features and security that come with it.

It has been revealed that this just so happens to be the best time to choose secure cloud storage, too. pCloud’s Black Friday promotion runs from November 13 to November 28. Starting with the base 500GB lifetime storage plan, pCloud’s one-time price comes down to $159 – 43% off. The 2 TB plan is presently down to $379, while the massive 10GB lifetime plan is 61% off at $1,099. pCloud is also offering a bundled 3-in-1 option that includes 3TB of storage, a lifetime pCloud Pass subscription, and pCloud Encryption for $579.

Secure cloud storage has major advantages, and a one-time subscription for terabytes of storage is rare these days.

Be sure to follow pCloud on X, Facebook and Bluesky.

Latest Update: The charging mistakes that could ruin your Nintendo Switch's battery

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (644 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Don't let bad charging habits turn your battery from Super to Super Smashed.
  • As great as handheld consoles can be, from the familiar-feeling Switch 2 to the Steam Deck OLED that still holds up against other PC handhelds, their batteries really are their Achilles' heel.
  • On a long enough timeline, all Switch batteries are bound to degrade until your console is only usable when docked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Don't let bad charging habits turn your battery from Super to Super Smashed.

As great as handheld consoles can be, from the familiar-feeling Switch 2 to the Steam Deck OLED that still holds up against other PC handhelds, their batteries really are their Achilles' heel. There's only so much playtime you can squeeze out of any portable device, and the more powerful the console, the shorter that tends to be. Moreover, most recent handhelds aren't designed for quick battery replacement. It's doable — Nintendo even provides instructions — but it's not like slapping a few AAs into a flashlight.

On a long enough timeline, all Switch batteries are bound to degrade until your console is only usable when docked. It's just a fact of lithium-ion technology. But if you're careful about how you charge, you can prolong this fate. If you're lucky, you might push things off until Nintendo's next-gen console arrives, whether that's the Switch 3 or another innovation.

It has been revealed that mostly, this is a matter of how often you charge your Switch, and to what percentage. There are some additional factors to consider, though, and we'll touch on those so you can put the free Mario Kart 8 Deluxe Switch 2 patch through its paces.

Industry observers note that never let your Switch drain to zero. Lithium-ion batteries have a finite number of charge cycles, and letting the battery die burns through them faster. Granted, the number of cycles is going to be well into the hundreds for any device, even beyond the 800 mark in the case of the Switch 1. But as you progress towards the end of that limit, your battery is going to offer diminished capacity. Nintendo also warns that you should charge once every six months, if you're not actively using it, to avoid permanently losing the ability to charge.

Sources indicate that you should also avoid charging to 100% unless you need as many hours as you can get. That's because the optimal charge for lithium-ion batteries is both more than zero and less than full. On most devices, the rule of thumb is between 20% and 80%. On the Switch 2, though, Nintendo has added a Stop Charging Around 90% option, which you can find under System Settings. Just remember to toggle this off and wait a few minutes longer when you're heading out on a trip to maximize your time.

Another important factor is ambient temperature. Realistically, you may be unlikely to store or use a Switch beyond its official operating range, which is 41 to 95 Fahrenheit (5 to 35 Celsius). Charging in extreme heat can, however, accelerate capacity loss, so you might want to avoid leaving your console in sunlight for prolonged stretches, or charging outside in climates with intense summer heat. Notably, while extreme cold can have an impact, it shouldn't be permanent.

A Switch is a complex device with delicate electronics, and the battery is embedded inside, rather than in an easily accessible compartment. Making a mistake could break something critical. In fact, Nintendo strongly urges contacting its Customer Service department instead of doing things yourself, and there's no official DIY guide for any Switch 1 model.

While there is an official guide for the Switch 2, Nintendo notes that only consoles with the BEE-001(-01) marking contain user-replaceable batteries, as far as the organization is concerned. On top of that, you need Nintendo's BEE-003(-01) Battery Replacement Kit, a careful touch, and an electrically grounded surface. A large enough static shock could fry circuitry.

It has been revealed that the good news here is that if you charge your Switch properly, the odds of it surviving until your next upgrade without a battery swap are pretty good. It's more a question of whether anyone you pass it along to will enjoy the same luxury.

Googlebook gets a much-needed desktop polish with Chrome 157

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (575 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Androidcentral

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google is giving its fledgling Googlebook OS a hefty dose of desktop polish with the rollout of Chrome 157.
  • Since the launch of Googlebook for consumers earlier this fall, Google has been slowly smoothing out the rough edges of its fresh Android-meets-desktop platform.
  • The biggest changes are aimed at those who favor vertical tabs over Chrome’s traditional horizontal layout.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google is giving its fledgling Googlebook OS a hefty dose of desktop polish with the rollout of Chrome 157. The company has published the full changelog for the browser revision, which includes five major features and 22 under-the-hood fixes.

Since the launch of Googlebook for consumers earlier this fall, Google has been slowly smoothing out the rough edges of its fresh Android-meets-desktop platform. With Chrome 157 being the primary interface on Googlebook OS, the little desktop quirks — a right-click menu that doesn’t work correctly or a tab rail that refuses to stay fully extended — appear even more glaring than they would on a traditional laptop. This release directly addresses those day-to-day friction points.

The biggest changes are aimed at those who favor vertical tabs over Chrome’s traditional horizontal layout. Before, if a vertical tab rail collapsed, it was difficult to tell which pages were open without expanding the entire sidebar. That’s what Chrome 157 fixes with Auto-Expand Vertical Tabs on Hover, which pops open the rail temporarily when you hover over it with your mouse or trackpad. You move away, and it drops down again.

According to recent reports, you can also resize the vertical tab bar by hand to allow for longer page titles. This option requires you to disable auto expansion, but Chrome remembers your preferred width between browser restarts and fresh windows.

In a recent development, google has also simplified navigation of Chrome’s Settings. You can now bookmark or share individual sections such as Appearance and Privacy, as each settings page has its own URL. The browser’s Back and Forward buttons also function when navigating between settings pages.

According to recent reports, chrome 157 adds a persistent control bar when sharing browser tabs during video calls. If you’re presenting via Google Meet, you can stop sharing or switch to another tab without having to dig through menus.

In a recent development, the system's native Save As dialog is enabled by default for actions like saving images, links, and webpages. You have more control over the file names and destinations, including Google Drive and external storage.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

The other 22 improvements cover minor irritations. Right-click the address bar, and you get the standard desktop text editing menu. Press Ctrl+L and you get the entire URL with parameters. Chrome also fixes bookmark context menus, improves PDF translation, and allows downloaded PDFs to open directly in a browser tab.

Other fixes include external monitor selection for Google Slides, Picture-in-Picture media controls, web app navigation, and third-party Google Sign-In prompts that might freeze when dismissed. Contextual Search also receives a less intrusive privacy notice.

Sources indicate that this massive patch comes after last week's broader Chrome 157 launch and a huge system patch in November. The update doesn’t come with a slew of flashy additions, but its suite of practical fixes should make Google’s browser more comfortable to use.

The Bank Outage May Have Nothing to Do With Your Bank

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (714 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you were planning to do any banking today, good luck.
  • Customers of many major financial institutions experienced unspecified technical challenges on Monday as thousands of reports flooded the uptime-tracking website Downdetector.com from people saying that they had issues using their banks in some way.
  • Sources indicate that it is right now unclear which systems are having challenges.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you were planning to do any banking today, good luck.

Customers of many major financial institutions experienced unspecified technical challenges on Monday as thousands of reports flooded the uptime-tracking website Downdetector.com from people saying that they had issues using their banks in some way.

Sources indicate that it is right now unclear which systems are having challenges. However, the problem may stem from technical difficulties at JPMorganChase, the top retail bank, which holds over 10 percent of all US deposits.

“JPMorganChase has experienced a temporary glitch related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems—there is no evidence this is cyber-related,” states JPMorganChase spokesperson Pablo Rodriguez. “It is taking longer than usual to service some customers.”.

Rodriguez adds that the bank is not experiencing a “systemic matter” but that “other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us.” The spokesperson adds that customers “still have access to their accounts and funds” and that the bank is working to resolve the issues.

It has been revealed that apparent complications with the banks, credit unions, fintech apps, and credit card companies appear to begin around 9:30 am ET and peaked at around 2 pm ET. Many people also reported issues using Zelle, the peer-to-peer money-transfer system adopted by major banks. However, in a statement, Zelle denied its systems were the cause of the reported outages while acknowledging that issues at banks may impact people’s ability to use Zelle.

It has been revealed that “Zelle is not down. Zelle is operating as it should,” a Zelle spokesperson states in a statement. “Consumers use Zelle through participating banks and credit unions, which manage their accounts and hold their funds. Consumers do not have a separate Zelle account, and Zelle does not hold consumer funds.”.

US Bank spokesperson Jeffrey Shelman also indicates the financial institution’s systems “are not directly impacted.” Shelman adds, however, that “clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.”.

Recent findings suggest that seth Eisen, senior vice president of communications at MasterCard, states, “Our network is operating normally.” A Visa spokesperson says the firm is aware of the payments concern, but that Visa’s systems are operating normally. A Capital One spokesperson similarly says the firm “has not been impacted and continues to operate normally at this time,” while a Bank of America spokesperson says its systems “have been operating normally today.”.

According to reports on Downdetector, which is sourced to user reports rather than official statements and may not be accurate, the issues on Monday also impacted customers of Wells Fargo, TD Bank, Navy Credit Federal Union, and more. These companies did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Eisen, the Mastercard VP, says that DownDetector was “not correct” in the case of his tech giant.

Industry observers note that whatever the cause, the timing of the challenges may as well have been designed to get people looking for broader patterns. Last Thursday, Microsoft 365 experienced an unprecedented 24-hour outage that impacted millions of people, governments, businesses, and other institutions globally. Microsoft executive vice president Charles Lamanna said in a post on X on Monday that the outage, which impacted Outlook, Teams, and many other Microsoft cloud services, was related to an update that started rolling out in July but only began causing problems last week.

According to recent reports, soon after Microsoft resolved its outage on Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop order. This time, the issue was related to a problem with Air Traffic Control’s communications systems. “The FAA’s legacy equipment became unstable when data began flooding the FAA FTI network, at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds,” the agency wrote in an FAQ explaining the outage. “This disrupted the system and created instability with aircraft communications and radar feeds.”.

The FAA’s five-hour ground stop resulted in thousands of canceled flights and otherwise disrupted travel for countless travelers. The impact of Monday’s banking outage remains unclear.

Updated 11/16/2026 at 5:18 pm ET: Added a statement from Capital One and additional context around Downdetector reports.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

JPMorgan Chase reported a "technical issue" that was affecting some consumer banking services Monday.

The bank said a "temporary glitch related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems" was causing some customer transactions to take longer than usual, though it said customers can still access their accounts and funds.

"There is no evidence it is cyber-related," a JPMorgan spokesperson said in a statement to CNBC.

Recent findings suggest that "This is not a systemic issue — other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us," the spokesperson stated. "We're working diligently to resolve this by the end of the day today.".

CNBC's Eamon Javers reported there was no indication of bad actors involved.

Still, other major banks were listed in outage reports as transactions between Chase and other institutions appeared to get held up. Consumers reported errors as early as 11:30 a.m. ET.

A representative for U.S. Bank mentioned that company was "not directly impacted. However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.".

Recent findings suggest that zelle is the peer-to-peer payments system backed by many of the largest U.S. banks, including JPMorgan.

The outage reports come days after separate, widespread problems with Microsoft Outlook and communication systems used by air traffic control centers.

— CNBC's Leslie Picker contributed to this report.

Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death gets at the heart of how influencers are radicalizing impressionable men.﻿.

Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death gets at the heart of how influencers are radicalizing impressionable men.﻿.

Industry observers note that before Clavicular and other manosphere streamers were introducing young guys to the concept of breaking their facial bones to become more attractive, there was an older generation of creators building massive followings with content focused on chemical biohacking. Were it not for steroid-obsessed influencers like Anthony “Tony Huge” Hughes launching YouTube channels over a decade ago, looksmaxxing might not have become such a prominent part of the digital media landscape in 2026. These creators became internet famous by presenting themselves as peak male specimens. But their larger-than-life online personas often concealed the truth about how sinister and toxic this kind of influencing can really be.

Sources indicate that hughes is the gravitational center of Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death — Hulu’s new three-part docuseries from director Stacey Lee. The series is both a deep dive into Hughes’ strange life and a fascinating exploration of how perilous the creator economy can be in the age of manosphere and looksmaxxing influencers. Through Hughes’ ever-expanding orbit of creators, Lee is able to highlight how lonely, impressionable men are all too easily radicalized by what they see and post online. And it makes clear that all these men are trapped in a deadly psychological prison of their own making.

Recent findings suggest that get Huge takes some time to touch on Hughes’ former life as a bankruptcy lawyer and supplement salesman who was investigated by the FDA for hawking unapproved performance-enhancing drugs. But most of the series takes place in Pattaya, Thailand, where Hughes spends his days producing content showcasing his extravagant life of nonstop partying and injecting substances that swell his muscles to huge proportions. Hughes takes pride in his image as a man with access to a harem of women, and the fact that his money gives him power over many of the people around him. He presents himself as the ruler of a small kingdom — and his entire brand is built on the idea that he can show people how to become more like him.

The men caught in Hughes’ aspirational fantasy aren’t just stateside fans who’ll never reach his muscle-y heights. He is also marketing himself to other established bodybuilding influencers who might be interested in joining his inner circle by following him to Thailand. These include a menagerie of biohacking / manosphere influencers who became vital parts of Hughes’ operation over the years. Leo Longevity (legal name Laith Abdallah Algaz), Elon Muscular (his legal name isn’t revealed), and Connor Murphy all built sizable social media presences of their own. But they were each compelled to move to Pattaya and join Hughes’ entourage by a powerful desire to feel connected to something larger and more fulfilling than their individual followings.

As Get Huge features clips of Hughes’ videos — the bulk of which are now only featured on Rumble and X following multiple account bans on YouTube and TikTok — you can see that he’s trying to sell his audience on his highly specific way of life. Hughes’ own videos make it seem like he’s living his dream surrounded by people who revere him. But with each interview, Get Huge makes it clear that for all of his posturing, Hughes has been living in something of a nightmare — one where many of his disciples have died under mysterious circumstances.

In a recent development, as these men explain why they were drawn to Hughes, you get the sense that looksmaxxing culture is a direct response to the widespread disaffection that followed the last decade of interconnected societal shifts, from the #MeToo movement to Donald Trump’s presidencies. Hughes seems very much like an entrepreneur profiting from men’s loneliness by convincing them that their lives would be better if they were part of his community. As Get Huge first maps out Hughes’ friendships, they all appear to be anchored by an odd, sometimes envious, but genuine kind of intimacy. But as the documentary digs deeper into its subjects’ lives, it becomes hard to see them as anything but emotionally stunted men who perform cartoonish masculinity for one another in ways that are psychologically unhealthy and, at times, physically dangerous.

Recent findings suggest that part of what makes Get Huge such an unsettling watch is how relatively calm and collected Hughes and the other interviewees are as they begin to discuss how many people in their circle have died in recent years. Hughes and Murphy grow closer as friends following Algaz’s death in 2023, but they seem to bond by making Algaz the butt of the joke in content produced after his death. Simply by letting these men speak frankly about their social dynamics, Get Huge reveals the manosphere as a space in which connections built on mogging and the objectification of women can rapidly deteriorate into infighting and petty jealousy. Elon Muscular readily speculates that Murphy might have had something to do with Algaz’s death because Murphy openly jokes about it. And the entire situation becomes that much stranger and more grim when Get Huge reveals that Murphy drowned shortly after the series initially wrapped filming.

In a recent development, though the deaths in Hughes’ circle bring a dark whodunit energy to Get Huge, the documentary emphasizes how much peril comes as a part of existing in the looksmaxxing space. Rather than trying to solve the mystery of how Algaz died, the docuseries presents his story as a cautionary tale. He’s an object lesson in how this lifestyle can warp a person’s perception of reality in a way that ultimately cuts them off from the kind of help they really need.

What might be most disturbing about Get Huge is the way it ends. The series follows Hughes to a youth bodybuilding event where he talks up his less-than-legal products to a newly introduced group of boys — some as young as 13. To keep his momentum going, Hughes has to appeal to a new, younger audience that doesn’t understand how everything about looksmaxxing is a performance. Though the docuseries gives you the distinct impression that people like Murphy and Algaz felt a true belonging with Hughes, its closing shots call into question how genuine any of his connections with other bodybuilders really are. By juxtaposing the deaths of Hughes’ adult acolytes with his focus on turning children into fans, Get Huge paints a clear picture of how the manosphere’s promise of emotional connection often ends in a twisted kind of exploitation. And that extractive energy feels foundational to a culture that runs on people turning every aspect of their lives into content.

All three episodes of Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death are now streaming on Hulu and Disney Plus.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, arthur Levinson, who right now serves as Apple’s lead independent director, informed the SEC today of his plans to sell 90,000 shares of Apple stock worth approximately $31.8 million. Here are the details.

If you’ve been following Apple for a while, you likely know the name Arthur Levinson, as he served as the manufacturer’s chairman from 2011 until September of this year, when Tim Cook took over as executive chairman as part of the leadership transition that saw John Ternus become CEO.

Back in May, Levinson made headlines when he sold 250,000 Apple shares for approximately $71.2 million. Three weeks later, he sold another 50,000 shares for $15.55 million. On the same day, he also transferred another 65,000 shares as a gift. Still, he retained approximately 3.7 million directly held shares in the firm.

In a recent development, today, Levinson informed the SEC in a Form 144 filing of his prepares to sell 90,000 common shares with an aggregate market value of $31,765,885.00, though the disclosure did not specify how many Apple shares he currently holds. The shares are held in The Homeplace Trust, with Levinson acting as trustee and handling the proposed sale on the trust’s behalf.

Industry observers note that the filing lists all shares as acquired in cash on February 27, 2001, though it does not disclose how much Levinson originally paid for them. For reference, Apple stock was trading at approximately $0.29 per share on a split-adjusted basis on that date, compared to roughly $353 today.

Importantly, Apple has undergone three stock splits since then, meaning the 90,000 shares listed in the filing don’t necessarily correspond to the number of shares Levinson originally purchased in 2001.

According to the filing, the transaction was expected to take place today through Charles Schwab. However, it is worth noting that Form 144 is only a notice of a proposed sale, meaning the filing does not confirm that the transaction has already been completed.

#697. How to put your iPad in recovery mode (with and without a home button)

Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

How to put your iPad in recovery mode (with and without a home button)

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (544 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A failed upgrade or a forgotten passcode doesn't have to mean the end of your iPad.
  • In a recent development, many iPad problems can be fixed with a simple restart, but sometimes that's not enough.
  • Recovery mode also lets you connect your iPad to your computer to update it, or in the worst-case scenario, restore it to its factory default settings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A failed upgrade or a forgotten passcode doesn't have to mean the end of your iPad.

In a recent development, many iPad problems can be fixed with a simple restart, but sometimes that's not enough. Severe complications with the tablet's software can make it completely inoperable, and in these cases, putting the iPad in recovery mode might be your only option.

Recovery mode also lets you connect your iPad to your computer to update it, or in the worst-case scenario, restore it to its factory default settings. It's best to save recovery mode for when nothing else works, but when it's needed, it can mean the difference between a bricked iPad and one that works just like latest.

There are a few situations when you might want to use recovery mode. Major software updates can sometimes fail, leaving you with a partially installed revision that keeps your iPad from turning on. Your iPad might reboot itself continuously, or you might enter the wrong passcode too many times and get locked out. Your computer might also stop recognizing your iPad, or your iPad might show a screen prompting you to connect it to a computer.

Industry observers note that to put your iPad in recovery mode, first connect it to your computer with a USB cable, and open Finder on Mac or the Apple Devices app on PC. From here, the process differs based on whether your iPad has a home button or not. If it does, hold the home and the power button down at the same time. Eventually, your iPad screen will go black and then show the Apple logo. Finally, it will show the recovery mode icon: an image of a USB cable connecting to a computer. Now release the buttons.

Recent findings suggest that newer iPads, like the iPad Pro, don't have a home button, so you need to use the power and volume buttons instead. First press and release the volume up button and then the volume down button. Next, press and hold the power button, and keep holding it through the Apple logo until the recovery mode icon appears. Then let go.

At this point, you can use the Finder or Apple Devices on your computer to find your iPad. If the process worked, you should see a pop-up explaining that the iPad needs to be restored or updated. It's best to start with the upgrade option, which will allow your computer to reinstall iPadOS without affecting anything else stored on your device.

If this option is successful, you'll be able to use your iPad again without losing any data. If it doesn't work, though, you'll have to put it back in recovery mode and choose the restore option. This will restore the iPad to its factory settings, completely erasing your data in the process.

Industry observers note that you can restore everything from your most recent backup (if you have enough iCloud storage), but it's a far more disruptive process that should only be used as a last resort. If your iPad still isn't working after trying both options or you can't get it to enter recovery mode, it may be time to get it professionally repaired or shop for a newly introduced iPad.

#696. Latest Update: I tested iPhone Duo, Galaxy Z Fold 8, and Xiaomi 18 Fold cameras in Dubai – and the zoom gap is unreal

Latest Update: I tested iPhone Duo, Galaxy Z Fold 8, and Xiaomi 18 Fold cameras in Dubai – and the zoom gap is unreal

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2031 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Androidcentral

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that for the first time, Apple, Samsung, and Xiaomi are all fighting on the exact same turf: wider, passport-style book foldables built to feel natural both closed and open.
  • Both the iPhone Duo and the standard Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 rely on dual-camera systems – a primary wide sensor paired with an ultrawide – leaving every zoom step past 1x to sensor crops and computational upscaling.
  • Recent findings suggest that before the iPhone Duo rolled out, much of the criticism focused on Apple dropping the telephoto lens compared to its flagship Pro range.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that for the first time, Apple, Samsung, and Xiaomi are all fighting on the exact same turf: wider, passport-style book foldables built to feel natural both closed and open. In theory, that levels the ergonomic playing field. Once you open the camera apps, though, three wildly different hardware philosophies emerge.

Both the iPhone Duo and the standard Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 rely on dual-camera systems – a primary wide sensor paired with an ultrawide – leaving every zoom step past 1x to sensor crops and computational upscaling. Meanwhile, the Xiaomi 18 Fold squeezes a full Leica-engineered triple-camera array into its sleek frame, anchored by a 200MP main camera and a dedicated 50MP 3.3x optical periscope telephoto.

Recent findings suggest that before the iPhone Duo rolled out, much of the criticism focused on Apple dropping the telephoto lens compared to its flagship Pro range. Samsung was rightly lambasted for the same compromise just a few months earlier, but can a passport-size foldable actually offer it all?

To judge this and see how those hardware choices hold up in the real world, I took all three foldables around Dubai Marina from harsh midday sun through sunset, blue hour, and neon-lit nights.

Here is how they actually compare, starting with the specs on paper.

50MP, 80mm equivf/2.8, OIS3.5x optical zoom.

It's hard for a modern smartphone camera to take bad photos in good lighting, and all three foldables capture crisp, share-worthy photos. Yet each phone immediately reveals a distinct personality, starting with framing.

Both the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Xiaomi 18 Fold shoot at a wider 23mm focal length, while the iPhone Duo’s 26mm main lens crops noticeably tighter into every scene.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

The Ocean Empress yacht along the marina is a textbook showcase of how these three pipelines diverge.

Xiaomi’s Leica Vibrant profile produces the most inviting, rich-looking photo straight out of the camera, giving the red-mahogany hull and gold latticework warm depth without blowing out the silver skyscrapers behind it.

Samsung favors cooler tones and aggressive contrast, leaving the lower-left hull signage significantly darker, while Apple prioritizes balanced exposure across the entire frame.

Push dynamic range to the limit—like shooting from underneath a massive concrete bridge out into harsh midday sun—and the iPhone Duo’s computational HDR takes the lead.

Apple renders the shaded underside of the concrete arch smoothly and keeps the lower boat deck legible, trading away a bit of blue saturation in the bright sky. Samsung keeps the sky bluest, but crushes the bridge overhang into a flat, greenish-grey shadow. Xiaomi sits comfortably in the middle, holding better sky color than Apple while avoiding Samsung’s crushed shadows.

Recent findings suggest that switch to the ultrawide lenses, and we see further subtle differences, largely due to hardware choices. While Samsung (13mm, 0.5x) and Apple (14mm, 0.6x) deliver true sweeping ultrawide perspectives, the Xiaomi 18 Fold’s 17mm (0.7x) ultrawide is noticeably narrower – and slower at f/2.4, which impacts the amount of light it can capture.

Standing in front of Pier 7, that 4mm focal-length gap between Samsung and Xiaomi is dramatic: the Galaxy Z Fold 8 captures the entire skyscraper on the far left edge, whereas the Xiaomi 18 Fold slices it clean out of the frame.

Between the two wider shooters, Samsung gives you slightly more real estate and bolder blue skies, while the iPhone Duo handles harsh architectural reflections on the sunlit right-hand tower and deep shadows under the skybridge with noticeably better dynamic range.

If you care about zoom on a foldable, or you're actively considering these three devices, this is the entire ballgame.

Sources indicate that neither the iPhone Duo nor the standard Galaxy Z Fold 8 includes an optical telephoto lens, leaving both reliant on main-sensor digital crops. Do you actually need a dedicated telephoto lens, though?

The Xiaomi 18 Fold packs a native 80mm (3.3x) periscope telephoto – and it embarrasses the competition from 3x all the way out to 96x. Look no further: this is the passport-style foldable made for an actual pro camera experience.

Industry observers note that at 2x (46mm–52mm), all three phones lean on high-resolution main-sensor crops and look sharp enough for social media. Push past 3x, however, and the gap opens immediately.

In front of La Brasseria, the iPhone Duo actually outshoots the Galaxy Z Fold 8 at ~4x: even though Apple crops tighter to 4.5x (107mm) compared to Samsung’s 3.8x (92mm), the iPhone’s 48MP sensor crop resolves cleaner lettering on the red menu banners and crisper horizontal slats behind the sign, whereas Samsung’s denoising smears the striped awning into watercolor mush.

Then you switch to the Xiaomi 18 Fold’s 3.3x (80mm) periscope – and neither digital crop comes close. Real glass resolves individual threads in the awning fabric, crisp white diamond motifs, and clean metallic edges on the sign, staying remarkably sharp even pushed to 6.7x (160mm) and 9.6x (230mm).

Pushing to maximum range across the Marina skyline reveals an interesting reversal between Apple and Samsung at ~10x.

While Apple won at ~4x, its 11x (263mm) ceiling turns soft and muddy on the distant Grosvenor House spire, while Samsung’s 9.6x (230mm) AI reconstruction sharpens straight architectural lines, keeping the GH monogram and pyramidal latticework distinct.

Still, Xiaomi’s 9.6x (230mm) periscope shot easily beats both with natural, optical-grade clarity – and then keeps going to 29x (690mm), 58x (1380mm), and an outrageous 96x (2300mm), pulling usable detail out of a rooftop emblem that is barely a speck at 1x.

Once the sun drops over Dubai Marina, metering strategy becomes just as notable as sensor size – and Samsung’s auto-exposure makes some puzzling choices.

In a recent development, at night, Xiaomi and Apple trade blows on the primary lenses, depending on your taste. Dropping to 1/20s lets the Xiaomi 18 Fold hold sensitivity down at ISO 400, capturing a wide 23mm frame with rich contrast, deep water reflections, and well-tamed storefront screens.

The iPhone Duo (1/25s, ISO 500) lifts shadows more aggressively across the sandstone towers and walkway with virtually zero noise, though its tighter 26mm lens clips the right edge. Meanwhile, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 inexplicably fires at 1/98s and pushes sensitivity to ISO 2500, resulting in darker shadows and visible grain on close inspection.

This is a fairly common occurrence in Samsung smartphones, and I hope we'll see it addressed in upcoming releases.

Zooming in at night completely flips the daytime hierarchy between Apple and Samsung.

Looking down at the glowing teardrop lanterns in the plaza, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 clips the lanterns into blown-out white blobs at 1.9x and 3.8x, and when it finally tames the highlights at 9.6x (230mm), heavy noise reduction smears the pedestrians and cafe tables into a soft painting.

It has been revealed that by contrast, the iPhone Duo’s multi-frame HDR keeps the intricate geometric lattice inside every lantern crisp at 4.5x (107mm) and even 11x (263mm). Still, the Xiaomi 18 Fold’s dedicated 3.3x–9.6x periscope wins easily, resolving cleaner filigree, flowerbeds, and paving tiles than either digital crop.

Challenging indoor venues – dim lounges, heavy colored LEDs, and high-contrast backlit signage – expose how each brand handles mixed white balance and bright light sources.

Recent findings suggest that in a dimly lit lounge corner, Apple and Samsung prioritize highlight protection: both keep the white neon script ("We dont fit in either") sharp and legible while preserving rich color in the hanging fringe lampshades. Xiaomi takes the opposite approach, pushing 1/25s and ISO 1600 to illuminate dark velvet curtains and doorways that disappear into shadow on the others, though the neon tubing blooms noticeably more.

Flood a room in monochromatic red lighting, however, and Xiaomi’s color science shines. The Xiaomi 18 Fold (ISO 500) holds true, deep crimson across the ceiling ductwork and light pillars while keeping the floor and booths clean. The iPhone Duo stays close in color accuracy (aside from motion blur on a passing guest at 1/20s), whereas the Galaxy Z Fold 8 (ISO 1250) shifts the red LEDs noticeably toward hot pink and magenta.

Similarly, facing the heavily backlit CARGO reception wall, Xiaomi wins on both framing and dynamic range – keeping the full "SINCE 2014" wall lettering intact on the left (which Apple’s 26mm lens crops off) while controlling the orange-white halo glow around the block letters with the cleanest shadow detail.

All three phones handle a tricky portrait cutout along the Marina promenade – cleanly separating the triangular gap inside a bent arm resting on the metal railing without accidentally blurring the bar itself.

Xiaomi takes the crown with creamy, optical-looking Leica bokeh and warm, flattering skin tones against the sunlit towers. The iPhone Duo is a close second, lifting facial shadows slightly brighter in a tighter 26mm crop, while the Galaxy Z Fold 8 applies more conservative background blur – offset somewhat if you enjoy Samsung’s signature Color Point monochrome-background effect.

Color Point is my favorite portrait mode feature on any device, and it's available on all Samsung phones, making it particularly useful regardless of the Galaxy hardware you buy.

In a recent development, one of the key benefits companies promote for buying a foldable is its form factor and its ability to use the rear cameras to take selfies. This is also used to argue that foldables don't need the best selfie-camera hardware, or, in the case of the iPhone Duo, can use under-display cameras.

Take this final comparison with a grain of salt, as it wasn’t the most scientific test. Still, it highlighted two practical realities of shooting selfies on foldables.

First, on the cover cameras, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 wins two-person selfies effortlessly: its wider 23mm lens fits both people comfortably, handles harsh overhead sunlight without washing out, and keeps both faces sharp.

In a recent development, the Xiaomi 18 Fold keeps both people in focus too, but suffers from heavy backlight flare when the sun sits behind your shoulder. Worst of all, the iPhone Duo crops tight at 28mm and falls straight into Apple’s single-subject portrait trap – keeping me sharp while completely blurring out my mom standing just inches behind me.

Sources indicate that second, if you want to bypass those f/2.2 cover sensors and use the much better rear cameras for selfies, Apple makes the experience unnecessarily frustrating. Unlike Samsung and Xiaomi – which put full camera controls right on the cover screen and let you trigger a timer simply by showing your palm – the iPhone Duo gives you no on-screen controls on the outer display and no palm gesture. Trying to awkwardly grip an unfolded foldable one-handed while stretching your fingers to press the Camera Control button or volume keys almost guarantees camera shake.

In a recent development, it's unlikely a single phone wins in every part of this comparison, so which phone wins overall? Here's how they ranked overall.

These results won't come as a huge surprise. While Apple, Samsung, and Xiaomi have all converged on wide, passport-style foldables, their camera hardware choices split them decisively in real-world shooting.

Xiaomi 18 Fold proves that foldables need a telephoto.

By opting for a dedicated telephoto lens and offering considerably better all-around hardware, the Xiaomi 18 Fold proves that a slim passport-style foldable can deliver a pro-like camera.

Industry observers note that the iPhone Duo takes a solid second place due to reliable point-and-shoot HDR, strong ultrawide performance, and cleaner night highlight retention than Samsung. As for Samsung, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 wins a couple of categories, but overall, it still has work to do to keep pace with its rivals.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, leopold Aschenbrenner's artificial intelligence-themed hedge fund Situational Awareness, which nearly collapsed in July, loaded back up on AI stocks as it returned to the financial markets at the end of the third quarter. But all of its holdings are down major the last month and a half.

According to a new regulatory filing, as the fund got back on its feet Aschenbrenner took an equity position in Australian neocloud organization SharonAI valued at more than $440 million, along with equity stakes in AI-centric plays Cleanspark, IREN, Bitdeer Technologies and Fermi. The Cleanspark stake is worth almost $39 million, while Iren and Bitdeer stakes are more than $21 million and more than $20 million, respectively. Fermi, meanwhile, has a value of more than $11 million.

The fund also owned call options at the end of September in neocloud Nebius, memory chip name Sandisk, the Roundhill Memory ETF (DRAM) and data center power play Bloom Energy. Sandisk and Nebius were key holdings that almost took out his fund over the summer.

It has been revealed that all of these Situational Awareness holdings have been routed since Sept. 30. SharonAI is at the top of that list, seeing a 58% loss in October. It's also fallen 11% so far this month. IREN was down 41% in October, while Nebius declined 35%. Last week, Nebius plummeted more than 16% in a single day after the firm issued a weak full-year forecast.

It's not known whether the hedge fund manager got out of those positions during the October AI selloff. The 13F filing is just a snapshot of what the hedge fund held at the end of the quarter.

Aschenbrenner — who rolled out the fund in 2024 after rising to fame that same year with his AI manifesto also entitled Situational Awareness — re-entered financial markets a bit in September, sources told CNBC at the time.

The Monday filing highlights he picked up right where he left off.

According to recent reports, the near-collapse of his hedge fund over the summer forced him to sell all of its public equity positions to Ken Griffin's Citadel. The fund had $45 billion in assets at its peak, but that tumbled to around $10 billion, consisting mostly of private stakes.

Recent findings suggest that stocked tethered to the AI trade took a hit in the most recent quarter as investors grew concerned about a slowdown in development of the technology. Those fears were spurred by comments from industry leaders such as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman back in September, with the latter saying that the company going public this year would be "ill-advised.".

Since then, pressure on the trade has only continued.

In recent weeks, investors have worried about how Democratic wins in the midterm elections could hinder data center development, whether some technology companies are using too much debt to finance the AI buildout and what role Nvidia will play in that financing with Jensen Huang now out as CEO at the company.

Losses in Nvidia as well as other AI-related stocks dragged down the three leading U.S. indexes during Monday's session as investors continued to assess the fallout of Huang's departure.

#693. Whether it's Black Friday or a CEO scandal, NVIDIA GPUs just don't get deep discounts

Whether it's Black Friday or a CEO scandal, NVIDIA GPUs just don't get deep discounts

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (775 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you're hoping for a cheap RTX card this November, the memory market has other aims.
  • Jensen Huang threw in the towel on November 12, resigning as NVIDIA's CEO after founding the firm more than three decades ago.
  • With Black Friday less than two weeks away, people want to know whether they can get their mitts on some cheap NVIDIA.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you're hoping for a cheap RTX card this November, the memory market has other aims.

Jensen Huang threw in the towel on November 12, resigning as NVIDIA's CEO after founding the firm more than three decades ago. NVIDIA's market value subsequently fell below $4 trillion for the first time since July 2025 before the week was out, leaving the market in a state of flux.

With Black Friday less than two weeks away, people want to know whether they can get their mitts on some cheap NVIDIA. While some mean the stock, which closed at around $162 on Friday, others mean the RTX 5080 they've had their eyes on all year. Spoiler alert: only one price has fallen, and it'll take more than a CEO scandal to move the needle on the other.

NVIDIA's graphics cards were already selling way beyond their list prices before Huang's scandal began, because AI data centers have spent the year swallowing the memory those cards need. The RTX 5080, for example, debuted at $999 and now starts at $1,999. The RTX 5090 was $1,999 at launch and sells at close to $7,000 at the lower end. Black Friday has a long record of barely denting GPU prices, and this year retailers have even less room than usual.

NVIDIA's stock had already dropped by around 20 percent over five straight weeks of losses before its board opened an investigation into Huang on November 8. That included a 9 percent drop following the midterm results and ballot measures that could slow data center construction.

In a recent development, reports in late October then linked Jensen Huang to Alice Huang, a Singapore-based exec whom U.S. officials reportedly suspect of spying for China. He then admitted to an affair with Alice Huang on November 8. Four days later, Jensen Huang was out as NVIDIA CEO, and by Friday's close the organization had posted six consecutive weekly losses. That's its longest streak since 2012, with roughly $1.7 trillion in market value shed since early October.

It has been revealed that HSBC downgraded NVIDIA from buy to hold on November 13, cutting its price target from $365 to $170, arguing that the stock would languish until the organization names a permanent CEO. Colette Kress is acting as interim CEO in the meantime while continuing as CFO, a role she has held since 2013. Shares fell another 3.7 percent in premarket trading on Monday, a day before what will be NVIDIA's first-ever earnings report without Jensen Huang.

Data centers brought in the lion's share of NVIDIA's $96.2 billion in last-quarter revenue, accounting for $89 billion. That leaves $7.2 billion for everything else, gamers included. The cause is that memory makers have been focusing on AI chips, pushing up the price of GDDR7 memory that RTX 50-series cards need.

Sources indicate that during the crypto-era shortage of 2021, Ethereum miners were snapping up cards that'd otherwise have gone to gamers, causing prices to balloon. That Black Friday, the best GPU deals were 5 to 10 percent off prices that were themselves already way too high. A year later, the miners were gone. Crypto prices crashed in May 2022, and Ethereum's switch to proof-of-stake that September instantly wiped out GPU mining profitability on the network, yet retailers still sold the RTX 3080 at its $699 list price while calling it a Black Friday deal.

Industry observers note that even without miners competing for stock, Tom's Hardware saw no real GPU deals over the 2023 Black Friday weekend, and in 2024 RTX 4090s were selling above $2,000 against their $1,599 MSRP. By the run-up to last year's Black Friday event, some RTX 50-series cards had settled within $30 of their list prices, but the sales barely had an impact. A PNY RTX 5060 down $20 to $279 made Windows Central's list of NVIDIA deals, while the cheapest RTX 5090 PC Gamer could find was $2,700, $700 over the list price. Those were the best conditions for any potential GPU deals in five years, and they led to discounts measured in tens of dollars.

Retailers heading into Black Friday on November 27 are holding RTX 50-series stock bought at wholesale prices that NVIDIA's Chinese board partners raised again in November. Yes, a Black Friday sale could shave some margin off the top, but any deals will still only be a very modest cut at best from record GPU prices. NVIDIA's stock price, meanwhile, will keep reacting to the likes of earnings and the board's choice of successor. Its GPUs, however, answer to the memory market and the data centers buying up all the company's output.

Industry News: The 8 Best Movies to Stream Right Now (November 2026)

📅 18 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1483 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • November is here, the holidays are approaching, and it’s gotten cold outside—the perfect time of year to cozy up inside with some of the best films gracing streaming services.
  • This month, there’s plenty of Halloween hangover for horror fans, with viral sensation Backrooms making corridors and empty rooms unimaginably spooky on HBO Max, Thanksgiving carving out a spot for grindhouse connoisseurs on Hulu, and the transgressive Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma proving the genre can have brains and blood over on Mubi.
  • If you prefer your thrills giant-sized, look no further than Netflix, where the king of monsters can be seen stomping across Japan in the Academy Award–winning Godzilla Minus Zero.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

November is here, the holidays are approaching, and it’s gotten cold outside—the perfect time of year to cozy up inside with some of the best films gracing streaming services.

This month, there’s plenty of Halloween hangover for horror fans, with viral sensation Backrooms making corridors and empty rooms unimaginably spooky on HBO Max, Thanksgiving carving out a spot for grindhouse connoisseurs on Hulu, and the transgressive Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma proving the genre can have brains and blood over on Mubi.

If you prefer your thrills giant-sized, look no further than Netflix, where the king of monsters can be seen stomping across Japan in the Academy Award–winning Godzilla Minus Zero.

It has been revealed that elsewhere, the Earth itself is in peril in a double bill of animated spectaculars. A warning from the future arrives in the stunning time-travel fantasy Arco, taking viewers on an imaginative journey across centuries on Hulu, while The Day the Earth Blew Up on HBO Max places Looney Tunes icons Daffy Duck and Porky Pig as the planet’s last line of defense. (We’re cooked.).

Here are WIRED’s picks of the best movies to watch right now.

According to recent reports, drawing inspiration from the works of Sylvain Chomet and Studio Ghibli in equal measure, director Ugo Bienvenu has created an absolutely gorgeous piece of animation. This French science fantasy epic follows 10-year-old Arco (Oscar Tresanini in French, Juliano Krue Valdi in English), who time-travels from his home in 2932 in hopes of seeing dinosaurs. Instead, he crashes in 2075, a point where humanity is on the brink of destruction, the planet wracked by brutal storms, its resources all but exhausted, and humanity living in protective bubbles.

Aided by schoolgirl Iris (Margot Ringard Oldra, Romy Fay) and her robot caretaker Mikki, Arco desperately tries to repair his damaged time-suit to return home. However, between environmental devastation, a strange trio hunting him, and his very presence risking the timeline, Arco’s time might be up. Beautiful but somber, Arco is one of the best yet sadly most overlooked films of the year, animated or otherwise.

Industry observers note that what good is a kamikaze pilot who survives? That’s the question haunting Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki) at the end of WWII, outlasting both the conflict and an encounter with an impossible, dinosaur-like creature on an isolated island. Returning to a devastated Tokyo, the directionless, traumatized Kōichi forms a relationship with fellow survivor Noriko (Minami Hamabe), raising an orphaned baby together. Yet their ad hoc family life is put in the atomic-breath firing line of that strange monster he encountered years earlier, now mutated to colossal size by exposure to atomic tests and stomping angrily onto land. Without weapons, military, or even much of a functioning society, can a still-broken Japan possibly withstand the horror of Godzilla?

While Ichiro Honda’s original 1954 Godzilla was a towering reptilian metaphor for the unknown risks of unleashing nuclear weapons on the world, Godzilla Minus One sees director Takashi Yamazaki leap back almost a decade to explore themes of survivor’s guilt, national despair, and rebuilding community. It’s a kaiju movie with brains, but also a treat for the eyes; it won the Academy Award for Best Visual Effects. With sequel Godzilla Minus Zero in cinemas now, it’s well worth catching up on before seeing Major G throwing down with arch-nemesis King Ghidorah.

Recent findings suggest that when struggling furniture seller Clark (Chiwetel Ejiofor) finds a crack in reality in his store’s basement, he becomes obsessed with exploring the seemingly infinite liminal space he’s slipped into. The space goes on forever, yet appears to be entirely empty—apart from an unseen presence stalking him. Becoming obsessed with mapping the unmappable, Clark’s already-fraying life disintegrates further, until his fixation ends up dragging his concerned therapist Mary (Renate Reinsve) into the Backrooms herself—except she doesn’t find it quite so uninhabited. And all the while, someone outside is watching closely.

From internet folklore to cinematic sensation, director Kane Parsons’ Backrooms was the surprise horror hit of the summer. It’s easy to see why—the endless sprawl of impossible corridors and uncanny rooms that connect in ways that seem to defy physics and geometry alike is darkly mesmerizing for viewers, while the unexplained nature of this twisted reality keeps you guessing at every turn. A sequel is in the works, but you can get lost in the Backrooms right now.

In a recent development, when up-and-coming director Kris (Hannah Einbinder) is hired to reboot the floundering Camp Miasma horror franchise, she wants to bring back Billy Presley (Gillian Anderson), the series’ original “Final Girl.” Unsettlingly, Kris finds Billy now living on the abandoned campsite from the dated first flick, living a reclusive life and obsessed with Little Death, the iconic killer from the series. Pitch meetings soon turn into the pair bonding over their fascination with, and experience of, the series—before descending into … well, the hint is in the film’s title.

A festival darling, picking up awards at both Cannes Film Festival and San Sebastián International Film Festival, this smart, transgressive horror outing from director Jane Schoenbrun (We're All Going to the World's Fair, I Saw the TV Glow) cleverly deconstructs the slasher genre and reexamines it from a queer—and extremely meta—perspective.

Somehow, despite a near-century of Looney Tunes cartoons (counting from 1930’s “Sinkin’ in the Bathtub”), The Day the Earth Blew Up is the series’ very first feature-length, fully animated movie (no, Space Jam doesn’t count). It’s been worth the wait, though—this loving pastiche of sci-fi B-movies is a stellar showcase for its top-billed stars, Daffy Duck and Porky Pig (both phenomenally voiced by the sadly departed Eric Bauza).

Industry observers note that with an asteroid hurtling toward Earth, UFOs flying around, a sinister scientist meddling with unknown substances, and a zombie plague spread by infected bubble gum, Earth’s last hope is a deranged duck and an anxious pig. We’re probably doomed, but at least we’ll die laughing—this hilarious outing is a reminder of everything great about these beloved characters.

When Yu Kobayashi (Yuzu Aoki) transfers to a upcoming school in rural Japan, he finds the strict culture and rigid conformity of students and staff alike unusual. Classes stand and bow to teachers in unnaturally uniform movements, PE lessons are precise marching practices, and even the hierarchy of bullies and victims seems oddly organized. Initially, Yu writes it off as culture clash in a new environment, until students inexplicably start to form ever-larger human pyramids, with teachers brutally encouraging them. Only Yu and outsider Ai Sato (Anna Yamada) seem able to resist the compulsion to join the pyramid—but with the increasingly maddening adherence to peer pressure spreading across Japan, they might be the only ones.

In a recent development, director and writer Yûta Shimotsu expands the almost surreal setup into an exploration of conformity and expectations, infusing it all with an uncomfortable dose of J-horror. It’s exceedingly weird in places and demands you make your own conclusions, but at a brisk 81 minutes, it’s a short, sharp, and frequently shocking slice of satire.

Every holiday deserves a related slasher flick—everything from April Fools’ to Christmas to, of course, Halloween. Thanksgiving had been the odd one out, until 2007’s Grindhouse (the anthology double feature coheaded by Robert Rodriguez and Quentin Tarantino), which featured a bunch of mock trailers, including one by Hostel director Eli Roth, centered on a killer Pilgrim. Fast forward to 2023, and Roth finally got the idea out of his head with this full-length version.

Industry observers note that A year after a Black Friday riot ends up with a body count, Plymouth, Massachusetts, finds itself stalked by a masked serial killer soon dubbed “John Carver.” The victims: anyone connected with the retail massacre—but the twisted chain of connections between Carver and his kills keeps viewers on their toes throughout. Thanksgiving is unapologetically loyal to the genre, but manages to cram in some sledgehammer-subtle commentary on consumerism alongside the gloriously gratuitous schlock.

When Alma (Maren Eggert) meets Tom (Dan Stevens), he seems perfect. Intelligent, poetic, able to dance—a rare modern gentleman. That is, until he starts glitching, revealing himself as an advanced robot. Initially repulsed, Alma is drawn into a three-week trial of a repaired Tom, testing his capabilities as an assistant and his capacity for emotion. It’s a quietly disconcerting experiment to watch play out, with Alma drawing closer to Tom almost in spite of herself.

First released in 2021, when undetectable AIs and synthetic humanoids were still just about within the realm of fiction, this German sci-fi drama now feels ahead of its time. While I’m Your Man bears some similarities to Alex Garland’s Ex Machina, it’s not as pre-apocalyptic, with director Maria Schrader balancing quasi-romcom tropes with hard existential questions about the nature of intelligence, the quiet banality of AI and robotics infiltrating society, and how we as humans respond.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia interim CEO and longtime CFO Colette Kress is about to have one of the biggest days of her career on Tuesday when the company reports its third-quarter results.

For the first time, Kress will be running through the numbers and sharing guidance without Nvidia’s charismatic but now-disgraced founder Jensen Huang.

Huang was forced to resign last week after he admitted to having an affair with an exec of a customer, Alice Huang, a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy, and he was accused of having two more affairs with Nvidia employees.

It has been revealed that now, the organization is facing questions about its restricted chips allegedly being smuggled into China, especially by Huang’s mistress’ company. Nvidia promised to conduct an internal investigation. Meanwhile, Huang was commanded to answer questions to Congress in a closed-door joint session with three Republican-led committees. Plus, top Democrats have also vowed to investigate the company.

Given the turmoil Nvidia is in, there are a number of questions that Kress should answer.

Huang’s role now and going forward. Huang ran Nvidia with an iron fist, having some 60 direct reports and his fingers in everything. No one knows the organization better than him.

Recent findings suggest that an internet petition signed by 180,000 and growing is calling for the board to reinstate him. Huang may also have been mounting an attempt to return, Financial Times reported. However, CNBC is reporting, citing unnamed sources, that the company is not in talks to reinstate Huang.

So, we’ll be looking for language from the interim CEO about Huang’s ongoing involvement with the company, its search for a new CEO, and any talks to bring him back.

Industry observers note that china and Singapore. As Huang vehemently argued in favor of easing export restrictions for Nvidia chips to China, Huang said that he’s seen no evidence that its powerful semiconductors were being diverted from legit buyers to China.

Sources indicate that but in October 2025, The New York Times reported that the U.S. was investigating Huang’s mistress’ company, Megaspeed, over allegations it was doing just that. Nvidia at the time vouched to CNBC that Megaspeed was legally using the chips for its cloud. However, Nvidia recently told The Wall Street Journal that it had voluntarily blocked Megaspeed from receiving more chips way back in June 2025.

Last year, Nvidia noted that Singapore, the region where Megaspeed is located, was one of its fastest-growing, accounting for 22% of its total revenue for its second quarter of that year. After the investigation into Megaspeed came to light, Nvidia changed how it reported revenue. It now reports based on a organization’s headquarters, instead of its shipping address. That completely hid sales to Singapore and Megaspeed’s impact.

So we’re listening to what Kress says about the future of sales to the China region and the cloud business in Singapore that was once 20% of sales. We’re especially listening for what she says about Nvidia keeping track of where its restricted chips wind up.

China sales policy. Huang’s argument was, essentially, that the U.S. can’t stop China from developing advanced AI models, so the West is better off selling them less powerful Nvidia chips and keeping them dependent, he stated on the Dwarkesh Podcast last summer. Notably, that’s a position that would make Nvidia a lot of money.

Recent findings suggest that the China hawks counter that selling an adversary any powerful chips at all will help them, and U.S. companies shouldn’t do that. So we’re listening for any indications that Kress is reversing Nvidia’s goals with China.

Bankrolling the AI build-out. The expectation is that Kress, the CFO who reportedly had unsuccessfully tried to push back against Huang’s extreme AI dealmaking, will be conservative on such deals going forward. We’ll be listening for what she claims about the impacts of existing deals on the books. (Will she subtly try to throw Huang under the bus for those controversial deals?) We’ll also be listening for her future plans.

Sources indicate that governance. With the ousting of Huang and more fallout sure still to come, has the board learned its lesson about too much power in the hands of one person? We’ll be listening for information about how Nvidia might restructure itself.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you like playing daily word games like Wordle, then Hurdle is a great game to add to your routine.

There are five rounds to the game. The first round sees you trying to guess the word, with correct, misplaced, and incorrect letters shown in each guess. If you guess the correct answer, it'll take you to the next hurdle, providing the answer to the last hurdle as your first guess. This can give you several clues or none, depending on the words. For the final hurdle, every correct answer from previous hurdles is shown, with correct and misplaced letters clearly shown.

An important note is that the number of times a letter is highlighted from previous guesses does necessarily indicate the number of times that letter appears in the final hurdle.

#686. Three small failures combined to take down Microsoft 365

Three small failures combined to take down Microsoft 365

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (758 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A hidden defect in Microsoft’s cloud gateway, dormant since July, was to blame for one of the largest outages in the manufacturer’s history last week.
  • Microsoft’s preliminary report places the outage between November 12 at 16:20 UTC and November 13 at 16:10 UTC, just under 24 hours total, and additional monitoring remained in place for any affected systems through November 14.
  • The outage started on November 12 and rapidly rippled through businesses and public offices that depend on Microsoft’s cloud and email exchange infrastructure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A hidden defect in Microsoft’s cloud gateway, dormant since July, was to blame for one of the largest outages in the manufacturer’s history last week. A preliminary Post-Incident Report (PIR) released by the company outlines how the latent bug, changes in traffic, and reduced server capacity combined to knock much of Microsoft 365 and Exchange infrastructure offline at the end of last week. Microsoft’s report lists the incident’s final status as “a technical glitch not related to cyber or AI/agents.”.

Microsoft’s preliminary report places the outage between November 12 at 16:20 UTC and November 13 at 16:10 UTC, just under 24 hours total, and additional monitoring remained in place for any affected systems through November 14.

The outage started on November 12 and rapidly rippled through businesses and public offices that depend on Microsoft’s cloud and email exchange infrastructure. The outage is covered in Microsoft’s incident IDs EX1550543 and MO1550821. You need Microsoft 365 admin credentials to see the full report on the company’s status pages, but Office Watch has reproduced the preliminary report, and the University of Pennsylvania maintains an archive of Microsoft’s service-health updates.

In a recent development, microsoft attributes the outage to three factors. A change deployed to Microsoft’s cloud gateway starting in July created a bug where, under certain conditions, CPU and memory resources could become exhausted and unresponsive. Microsoft contends that the defect was never discovered in pre-release testing because the hardware used was less powerful than some systems already deployed in production, where higher CPU core counts on newer machines apparently contributed to the lockout.

It has been revealed that the second factor was server load. Microsoft said that “Traffic shifts during standard network maintenance and upgrades exposed a latent bug.” The company keeps two independent gateway systems in place to access Microsoft 365 for resilience. If one system encounters trouble and users can’t get through the front door, the other is opened to keep traffic flowing. According to the report, about 15 hours prior to the outage, traffic from Teams was shifted from the alternate gateway to the primary, where Exchange Online access is maintained. The switchover was a standard fail-safe, but it left the gateway handling more traffic, with a different mix of requests than before. As requests continued to pile up, affected servers exhausted their capacity and refused latest connection requests.

The traffic shift exposed a third factor: infrastructure capacity. An existing fault meant that Microsoft’s gateway server fleet was operating at 14 percent below optimal conditions. That missing headroom could have normally absorbed the demand, but when combined with the changed traffic patterns and underlying defect, it left the gateways with lock contention as requests kept piling up.

Industry observers note that as US business operations began hitting their daily peaks, the gateway servers began to freeze. Backup systems that shifted requests away from unresponsive servers did their job, but were met with the same lockouts on the supposedly healthy backup gateways. This created a snowball effect, leaving more than 80 percent of Microsoft’s affected gateway servers frozen in the sweep. Mechanisms in place to isolate affected systems by region seem to have failed. Microsoft’s current report doesn’t address why these isolation systems may have failed.

Recovery took longer than normal because the fix required a targeted system upgrade from Microsoft engineers. Attempts to restart the gateway servers were ineffective; when the servers came back online, large request queues were still waiting for access, immediately triggering the same resource exhaustion that contributed to the outage in the first place. Microsoft says that services like Teams, OneDrive, and other Office applications could be routed away from the affected infrastructure, but scaling limitations stopped Exchange Online from making a similar move.

Since the bug from July was still undiscovered, system rollbacks were equally ineffective. Simply returning to a previous state where things were “working” couldn’t happen, because the ghost was already in the machine. Servers were patched and returned to service gradually, and Microsoft says it has added additional capacity and traffic-distribution guardrails to try to avoid anything similar happening again. Microsoft also extended delivery timeouts on affected emails to stop delayed messages from bouncing back as undeliverable.

Microsoft expects to publish its full final incident report on November 20. This final report may provide additional clarification on why the regional isolation systems failed and what corrective actions will be taken to ensure this type of outage can be avoided in the future. All of Microsoft’s cloud services appeared online and operational as of Monday morning.

#685. The important Gmail security settings you should be using
