The companies say this is a technical problem and not a cyberattack.

According to recent reports, customers of multiple banks and financial services are reportedly experiencing service disruptions today. Chase, Bank of America, US Bank and Wells Fargo were the top four services with challenges reported on Down Detector at 3PM ET, but Zelle, Capitol One, PNC, JPMorgan and Truist were seeing spikes in unavailability. The number of reports began increasing for some banks around 10AM ET, while others didn't begin spiking until the afternoon.

A representative from Chase told the Associated Press that customers might be seeing slower transaction times "due to a technical matter," and added that it was not a cybersecurity problem. The publication also heard from a spokesperson for US Bank who mentioned clients might see delays for sending or receiving payments through Zelle.

Sources indicate that the service interruptions for these financial institutions follows on multiple headline-grabbing technical challenges. Several Microsoft services went down on November 12. The following day the US Federal Administration Authority issued a ground stop for all flights in the country following a problem with air traffic control equipment.

Hyperscale data centers use 2% of US electricity

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (668 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One flashpoint for the tech industry’s all-in push on Large Language Models has been the sudden rush to turn investment money into hyperscale data centers.
  • A latest study has tallied up energy use and estimated emissions for hyperscalers operating between May 2024 and April 2025 in the United States.
  • The team started with a list of 675 facilities from a commercial database based on news reports, company statements, and satellite imagery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One flashpoint for the tech industry’s all-in push on Large Language Models has been the sudden rush to turn investment money into hyperscale data centers. The rush hasn’t allowed anyone to plan how to supply the required electricity cleanly or with minimal impact on ratepayers. Instead, it has been difficult to even collect information on what’s being built.

A latest study has tallied up energy use and estimated emissions for hyperscalers operating between May 2024 and April 2025 in the United States. They weren’t able to differentiate between AI compute and more traditional data services, but it provides a clear point of reference that could be tracked moving forward.

The team started with a list of 675 facilities from a commercial database based on news reports, company statements, and satellite imagery. They dropped any that didn’t have a reported electrical capacity or that they couldn’t verify was a suitably large building with the expected cooling and electrical connection equipment. That reduced the list to 403 data centers with an average electrical capacity of about 40 megawatts.

In a way, that makes this a very conservative estimate, since 272 facilities believed to be large data centers were left out. But if you’re interested in AI data centers, specifically, it’s also true that some of the facilities included may not fall in that category.

That fact also introduces some uncertainty in the actual power usage of these data centers. Relying on other research, they use a range—some conventional data centers run at an average of about 48 percent of capacity, while AI training loads have been running higher, at around 70 percent.

Putting that together, the total power usage for the year by these 403 data centers was estimated at 68 to 99 terawatt-hours. That amounts to 1.5 to 2.2 percent of total US electricity use, on par with the total used by Wisconsin or Indiana.

A recent Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory report estimated the total electricity use of all data centers of any kind in the US (minus crypto mining) at 76 terawatt-hours in 2018. In 2024, that number was up to 192 terawatt-hours. That means the hyperscale data centers identified by this study account for something like one-third to one-half of all data center energy use.

The researchers also wanted to estimate the greenhouse gas emissions associated with generating all that electricity. It’s fairly straight-forward to get a reasonable number here—calculate the mix of generation in each data center’s region of the grid, and apply that CO2 per watt-hour rate to a data center’s electricity use.

This yields 21 to 31 million metric tons of CO2 for the year. That’s around 0.5 percent of total US fossil fuel CO2 emissions.

These data centers aren’t located in areas of especially clean energy—their energy mix was only slightly cleaner than the US average. About 54 percent of the electricity was generated by fossil fuel power plants (dominantly natural gas), with 25 percent from renewables, and 21 percent from nuclear.

In a recent development, this doesn’t include any “behind-the-meter” generation on-site, though. The xAI data center in Tennessee notably ran a fleet of natural gas turbines during this study’s time period, for example. Cleanview, which describes itself as a market intelligence firm, has tracked a boom in on-site generation since early 2025, including 116 current or planned data centers. While this may not affect this study’s numbers much, it is becoming increasingly significant over time.

This matters because the types of generators being used are much less efficient than utility power plants, emitting 60 to 80 percent more greenhouse gas to produce the same amount of electricity. (Conversely, if a data center built solar generation instead, it could reduce the carbon footprint of its energy.).

Although this study can’t pinpoint the energy use of AI data centers alone, repeating this analysis in subsequent years could reveal the growth related to the AI buildout—at least as long as that buildout lasts.

Nature Sustainability, 2026. DOI: 10.1038/s41893-026-01985-7 (About DOIs).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanksgiving is coming, and so, possibly, is an audience. If you want to show your in-laws you know how to entertain in style with a postprandial espresso or cappuccino, don’t be fiddling with steam wands and the owner’s manual while Uncle Bob stands nearby and offers his opinions (at full volume).

Industry observers note that luckily, there are plenty of early Black Friday espresso machine deals happening right now. If you take advantage, it will make you look smart both by not paying full price and by knowing how to pull a perfect shot, having had three weeks of practice.

Each deal below is on a machine a WIRED reviewer has tested—including a Breville that one colleague has used happily for seven years—and personally recommends. For more savings, check out our Best Early Black Friday Deals, as well as early deals at Amazon and Home Depot.

Updated November 16: I’ve removed expired deals and added new deals on De’Longhi, Ninja, Nespresso, and Atlas Coffee Club.

This sleek, design-oriented semiautomatic (“a steampunk gasworks of a thing,” according to former WIRED reviewer Matthew Korfhage) is quite dramatic in person, and it has a dual boiler—meaning you can froth milk at the same time you’re pulling a shot—and it comes with a nice set of accessories, including a tamper and milk pitcher. Note that this sale is on the 2nd Gen machine, which features expanded grinder settings and a newly introduced portafilter.

According to recent reports, formerly the Linea Classic, De’Longhi’s Classic is the best bare-bones espresso machine we’ve tried, with a pressure gauge, 15-bar pump, and updated thermoblock system. I used one for a full year and, while it’s not as foolproof as a semiautomatic, it was enough for morning espresso shots and cappuccinos, and I even pulled off some rudimentary latte art with its steam wand.

The Vertuo Pop+ is our favorite pod maker for espresso, and the Deluxe model adds a larger, side-mount water tank (37 ounces to the original’s 25 ounces) and fresh finishes, including this white one that’s on sale. (There’s also matte black-and-gold and a sort of gunmetal gray, but those are not as heavily discounted.).

We appreciated this semiautomatic’s slim profile, consistent shots, and built-in burr grinder. The cold-brew setting is more of a gimmick than a way to make actual cold brew, and some design choices are a little quirky, but it’s a beautiful, industrial-looking machine that takes up only 12 inches of counter space.

Ninja sometimes has a reputation for doing too much, but this semiautomatic we liked is a beginner-friendly option that pulls some solid shots. It’s got a built-in grinder and milk frother, the latter of which can make cold foam and even has a setting for plant-based milk. In true Ninja fashion, it also has settings for drip coffee and cold brew, but neither impressed our tester, so I wouldn’t buy it for that alone. (Note the sale is on the “Gunmetal” color only.).

Atlas (3-month Gift subscription).

Atlas (6-month Gift subscription).

Maybe you or your recipient already has an espresso machine; in that case, they’ll need some quality beans. Our favorite coffee subscription, Atlas Coffee Club, has a new gift option on offer for Black Friday, which is a quarterly subscription of three bags of unique, globally sourced coffee every three months for $59. You can choose any roast you want, including espresso roast and even Nespresso pods. If you’d rather buy an ongoing subscription for yourself, your first bag is free with Atlas’ Black Friday sale.
